name: Testosterone undecanoate injection (Aveed)

card.summary: Long-acting testosterone depot injection given in a clinic every few months; approved for deficiency, with a REMS programme for lung oil-embolism and anaphylaxis risk.
card.note: US product requires a REMS because of pulmonary oil microembolism and anaphylaxis risk.

quick.overview:
Testosterone undecanoate injection is a long-acting testosterone depot sold as Aveed in the US and Nebido in Europe. It is given intramuscularly in a medical setting and is approved for men with testosterone deficiency.

It is discussed in muscle and TRT communities as a way to avoid frequent self-injection. Published studies are in hypogonadal men; no trials examine it for appearance in healthy people.
quick.mechanism: The undecanoate ester is dissolved in oil and releases slowly from the muscle depot, where it is converted to testosterone. Intramuscular half-life is reported around 21 days in tea seed oil and 34 days in castor oil.
quick.risks: The FDA rejected Aveed three times (2008, 2009 and 2013) over concerns about pulmonary oil microembolism (POME) and anaphylaxis before approving it in 2014 with a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy. Other reported effects are acne, hypertension, raised liver enzymes and lipid changes. It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US.

lead: Testosterone undecanoate injection is a long-acting, oil-based intramuscular depot of testosterone, marketed as Aveed in the United States and as Nebido (and Reandron) in Europe, Australia and elsewhere [1]. The undecanoate ester is a prodrug: it is slowly released from the muscle depot and converted by blood esterases into ordinary testosterone, so the active hormone is the same one the body makes [1][10].

Its main appeal in medicine and in muscle and testosterone-replacement (TRT) communities is the schedule. Older esters such as enanthate need to be injected every few weeks, and reviewers have noted that this produces swings in mood, energy and sexual function between doses [10]. After two closely spaced loading injections, undecanoate is given roughly once a quarter in a clinic, which keeps blood testosterone in a physiological range across the interval [11]. For people who care about how they look, the connection runs through muscle, body composition, bone and energy: testosterone replacement in deficient men is associated with greater lean mass and bone mass [10][1].

The US route to approval was unusually long. The FDA declined the product in 2008, 2009 and 2013 over pulmonary oil microembolism (POME) and anaphylaxis, and approved it in March 2014 only with a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) under which it is administered by a trained provider in a healthcare setting [1]. It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US [1]. Published trials are in men with hypogonadism, delayed puberty and related conditions; none test it as a cosmetic intervention in healthy men [2][3][4][5][6].

paras: The labelled indication is testosterone replacement therapy in adult men with deficiency or absence of endogenous testosterone, in other words hypogonadism [1]. Reviews of the injection describe its use in primary (testicular) and secondary (pituitary or hypothalamic) hypogonadism, and in men whose low testosterone is associated with reduced muscle and bone mass, impaired sexual function and low energy [9][10].

Registered studies have also looked at the depot for erectile dysfunction in hypogonadal men, alone or alongside PDE-5 inhibitors [7], for pubertal replacement in boys with delayed puberty [6], for bone mineral density in Klinefelter syndrome [24], and for late-onset hypogonadism in older men [25][15].

Within physique-focused communities, testosterone undecanoate is mentioned mostly in the context of TRT and long-acting alternatives to frequent self-injection, rather than as a first-choice bodybuilding ester. Users who like the idea describe the appeal as fewer injections and steadier levels [18]; others on T Nation have said they prefer shorter-acting esters, noting that the undecanoate takes several injections to build up to steady levels [19].

The chain from the drug to appearance is indirect: replacement in men who are deficient is associated with gains in lean mass and bone, and with energy and drive that support training [10]. Wikipedia notes that the compound is also used for physique and performance enhancement and is controlled in many countries [1]. No published trial has tested it for appearance outcomes in healthy, eugonadal men.

Testosterone undecanoate is an agonist of the androgen receptor once converted to testosterone; Wikipedia describes the parent hormone as strongly androgenic with moderate anabolic effects [1]. The compound is the 17-beta undecanoate (undecylate) ester of testosterone, formula C30H48O3 [1].

Because the long fatty-acid chain makes the ester very lipophilic, it leaves the oil depot slowly. Reported intramuscular elimination half-life is about 20.9 days in tea seed oil and 33.9 days in castor oil, with mean residence times of roughly 35 to 36 days, compared with about 4.5 days half-life for testosterone enanthate in castor oil [1]. The marketed injectable is a solution in castor oil with benzyl benzoate [1].

A clinical study reported that plasma dihydrotestosterone stayed in the normal range in men on the long-acting injection [12]. Clinicians have also described a prolonged washout in men with congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism after stopping the depot, in which exogenous testosterone remained measurable for longer than expected [13], and a case report describes recovery of sperm production after treatment with clomiphene following long-term use [14]. Testosterone esters can be detected in blood tests used in anti-doping analysis [23].

Reported effects of testosterone undecanoate include acne, increased body and facial hair, voice changes, increased libido, hypertension, raised liver enzymes and raised triglycerides [1]. Testosterone therapy in general can suppress the body's own sperm production, a reason clinicians discuss fertility before starting [14]. Wikipedia's overview of testosterone therapy lists raised haematocrit, worsened sleep apnoea and prostate-related concerns among recognised issues [21].

The two events that shaped the drug's regulatory history are POME, in which oil droplets from the injection reach the lung vessels and cause cough, throat tightness or breathlessness, and anaphylaxis [1]. A 2023 literature review covering 29 studies and 7,978 patients identified eight studies reporting a total of 88 POME episodes or cough events, and cited one post-marketing review reporting 223 cases per 3,107,652 injections; where POME occurred almost all cases resolved within about an hour without intervention, and the authors concluded it was rare [9]. The US label's REMS requires administration and observation in a healthcare setting because of these risks [1].
Australian reports described an anaphylaxis case attributed to the benzyl benzoate excipient in Reandron 1000, and the manufacturer advised physicians to be aware of serious allergic reactions [1].

Questions about cardiovascular risk of testosterone therapy led the FDA to review the class in 2014, and in 2015 the agency said that benefits and safety for age-related low testosterone had not been established [21]. In February 2025 the FDA removed the cardiovascular wording from the boxed warning for testosterone products, citing the TRAVERSE trial, and added a warning about increased blood pressure [20][21]. A registered phase 4 trial of 673 hypogonadal men examined blood pressure effects of testosterone replacement [3].

In 1954 Ciba filed a Swiss patent for Triolandren, an injectable combination that included testosterone undecylenate, a precursor of the undecanoate, with a US filing following in 1955 [1]. Injectable undecanoate was in use in China for some years before oral products reached European markets in the late 1970s [1]. Testosterone itself was first isolated in 1935 and approved for medical use in 1939 [20].

Schering AG developed the depot formulation for hypogonadism, described in a 2004 drug-development profile [22]. Nebido received its first European approval in Finland in November 2003, the EU mutual-recognition procedure finished in July 2004, and commercial launches in Finland and Germany began in late 2004 and expanded through 2005 [1]. A 2005 review framed the product as answering a need for long-acting esters that deliver physiological levels without large fluctuations [10]; a 2007 review traces testosterone products from oral forms to long-acting injectables and depots [16]. A multicentre prospective study in Korean men with testosterone deficiency syndrome reported on efficacy and safety of the depot [15].

The FDA rejected the US version, Aveed, in 2008, 2009 and 2013 because of concerns over POME and anaphylaxis, and approved it in March 2014 after the manufacturer agreed to a REMS [1]. Aveed is marketed by Endo Pharmaceuticals according to the FDA label metadata [26]. Newer oral undecanoate capsules were approved by the FDA later: Jatenzo in March 2019, Tlando in March 2022 and Kyzatrex in July 2022 [1].

Testosterone undecanoate is prescription-only in most jurisdictions, a Schedule III controlled substance in the US and Schedule IV in Canada [1]. Testosterone is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's list of prohibited anabolic agents, and testosterone-related detection methods are used by anti-doping laboratories [20][23]. In the US, Congress classified anabolic steroids as controlled substances in 1990 [20].
Brand names include Aveed (US), Nebido and Reandron 1000 (Europe and Australia), and, for oral forms, Andriol, Jatenzo, Kyzatrex and others [1].

On T Nation, threads discuss Nebido and Aveed mostly among patients on TRT. One 2014 poster described asking an endocrinologist for Aveed because of the idea of injections only every ten weeks or so [18]. A 2017 thread from a man in Norway discusses being offered Nebido after a low testosterone test result [17]. A 2018 reply in another thread voices doubt about the depot, arguing that the undecanoate ester needs several shots before levels become steady and leaves the patient hypogonadal for the first months [19]. These are individual opinions rather than trial findings.

A 2025 registered trial is examining testosterone-induced muscle memory and its mechanisms [8], and a registered phase 2 study is planned in elderly frail men with testosterone deficiency [27]. Earlier registered work covers non-alcoholic steatohepatitis in hypogonadal men [28] and quality of life of men and their spouses on therapy [29]. Wikipedia lists further investigation of oral undecanoate formulations in liver disease [1].

A phase 3 long-term safety study (NCT00467870) enrolled 531 hypogonadal men receiving intramuscular undecanoate [2]. A phase 4 trial of 673 men examined blood-pressure effects of testosterone replacement [3]. A phase 3 trial of 96 hypogonadal males assessed long-term treatment [4]. A phase 4 trial of 34 participants tested the drug during simulated military operations with caloric restriction, exercise and sleep loss [5], and a small trial examined delayed-puberty replacement in 27 boys [6]. A 30-patient phase 4 study examined combination with PDE-5 inhibitors for erectile dysfunction [7].

A review of testosterone undecanoate for sexual dysfunction reported that after two loading injections six weeks apart, one injection about every twelve weeks was usually sufficient with levels in the physiological range, and described improved sexual function in a substantial number of elderly men with low levels [11]. A study in Klinefelter syndrome examined bone mineral density with replacement [24]. A 2013 osteoporosis study of lower-dose oral undecanoate in elderly men reported improved bone density [1]. A 36-month study in middle-aged men with metabolic syndrome and late-onset hypogonadism reported bone mineral density gains of about 5 percent per year [1].

For the wider class, the TRAVERSE cardiovascular safety trial of testosterone therapy led to the 2025 FDA labelling change [20][21]. No trial has tested the depot for appearance outcomes in healthy men.

lore.intro: Undecanoate depots appear in testosterone-replacement and muscle forums mainly as a convenience option, discussed alongside shorter-acting esters, with occasional skepticism about how quickly levels stabilise [17][18][19].

claims.claim: A quarterly injection gives steadier levels than injecting every week or two.
claims.believers: Patients on T Nation describe being attracted to the idea of a shot only about every ten weeks and to avoiding frequent injecting [18].
claims.experts: Reviews describe the depot as designed to avoid the swings seen with older esters and report levels staying in the physiological range between injections [10][11].

claims.claim: Undecanoate takes months to build to steady levels, leaving users deficient at the start.
claims.believers: One poster argues the ester needs a few shots to reach physiological levels, so the first months can be sub-par [19].
claims.experts: The product label and reviews describe two initial loading injections closely spaced to reach steady state, and the long half-life means accumulation over several injections [1][11].

claims.claim: The depot is too risky because of the lung 'oil embolism' reaction.
claims.believers: Posters who follow the regulatory history discuss the FDA's three rejections and the clinic-only REMS when weighing the depot, and a 2017 thread from a man offered Nebido after a low test result discusses his hesitation about it [17][18].
claims.experts: A 2023 review found POME reported rarely and usually resolving within about an hour, while US regulators require clinic administration and observation [9][1].

claims.claim: Undecanoate shots are a route to bodybuilding-level muscle.
claims.believers: Wikipedia notes that testosterone undecanoate is also used to improve physique and performance, and TRT-focused forum users discuss esters in terms of training and recovery [1][19].
claims.experts: Published trials are in hypogonadal men and boys with delayed puberty; none examine physique outcomes in healthy lifters with this depot [2][4][6].

claims.claim: Long-term use leaves a long washout and can delay recovery of natural production.
claims.believers: Forum posters describe long-acting esters as taking a long time to build up and to clear, which they weigh when choosing between esters [19].
claims.experts: A letter in men with congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism described unexpectedly prolonged washout, and a case report describes recovery of sperm production after long-term use with clomiphene [13][14].

angle.text: Testosterone undecanoate is a prescription testosterone replacement. In men with documented low testosterone, replacement is associated with greater muscle mass, bone density and energy, which people connect to training and body composition. Its distinguishing feature is the depot: visits a few months apart rather than frequent injections.
